oil.summary: A split tape today: Brent edged up 0.37% to $91.36/bbl for a fourth consecutive session of gains, while WTI slipped 0.60% to $84.40/bbl. The divergence reflects a tightening physical premium in Atlantic and Gulf grades as Hormuz traffic slows materially—two Chinese VLCCs made U-turns and are now idling in the strait, per Bloomberg ship-tracking data. Iran's stated condition that the strait remains closed until Washington meets interim deal terms, combined with blown-through diplomatic deadlines and new sanctions being weighed by the Trump administration, keeps the geopolitical bid alive. The standout move was RBOB gasoline, crashing 8.85% on the day and down over 11% on the month—likely reflecting crack-spread normalization from elevated refiner margins flagged in today's earnings commentary. Murban crude hit a four-month high on ADNOC supply curbs to Asia, and Russia's Q2 export revenues jumped 27%—a direct beneficiary of the war premium.
drivers: Hormuz disruption: Chinese VLCCs turning back, Iran vowing closure until US meets deal conditions
Diplomatic breakdown: US-Iran deadline missed, new sanctions and potential land blockade under consideration
RBOB gasoline collapsed 8.85% intraday—refiner crack spreads normalizing after wartime highs; distillate stocks falling per API data

gas.summary: Henry Hub firmed 2.85% on the day to $2.856/MMBtu, recovering modestly on the month after a -0.35% drag, while TTF slipped 1.42% to €62.74/MWh despite remaining up over 5% on the month. News flow is thin but pointed: the Iran conflict is visibly transmitting into consumer energy costs globally. UK household energy bills are set to rise 4% in October to a three-year high as the war tightens global gas supplies, and India is pivoting toward piped gas infrastructure to offset surging LPG costs driven by the same conflict. These demand-side substitution stories suggest durable structural pressure on gas markets even if near-term spot prices show mixed moves.
drivers: Iran war tightening global LNG/LPG supply chains, driving UK October energy bills to three-year highs
India accelerating piped gas rollout as a domestic substitute for elevated-cost LPG
Henry Hub +2.85% on the session; TTF easing slightly after a strong weekly and monthly run-up

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged up 0.65% to $77.91/EUA today but remain marginally negative on both a weekly and monthly basis, suggesting no fresh urgency in compliance buying despite the broader energy price shock. The dominant macro signal for the power sector remains the Hormuz closure: Iran has explicitly tied reopening to US deal concessions, leaving gas and oil supply risk elevated and undermining the case for lower European power-generation costs. TTF, the key marginal fuel-cost signal for EU power, is up over 5% on the month. Separately, Peter Thiel's $76 million stake in an Argentine Vaca Muerta operator and reports of the US quietly building an energy foothold in Iraq point to longer-term supply-diversification efforts, but neither has near-term power-market relevance. Data for this sector is relatively thin today.
drivers: Iran confirms Hormuz stays closed until US meets deal conditions—sustaining gas supply risk and upward pressure on EU power generation costs
EUA carbon flat to slightly positive; monthly trend still negative, suggesting muted compliance-buying urgency despite fuel-cost inflation
TTF +5.16% on the month remains the key marginal cost driver for European power; near-term headlines sparse for direct power-sector catalysts
